core: The core HR functions in a hospitality operation: recruitment, selection, onboarding/orientation, training and development, performance management, and retention
The industry's high employee turnover, with dated BLS leisure-and-hospitality quits/separations data relative to other sectors
Seasonality and variable 24/7 scheduling as structural drivers of turnover
Employee engagement, empowerment, and motivation, and how empowerment supports frontline service
The service-profit chain (Heskett, Jones, Loveman, Sasser, Schlesinger 1994) linking employee satisfaction to service value, customer loyalty, and profit
supporting: The cost of turnover (recruiting, onboarding, training, lost productivity, coworker strain) stated qualitatively
Manager coordination roles and dated BLS median wages for lodging and food service managers
The distinction between job satisfaction and engagement
outOfScope: Service-quality measurement theory (SERVQUAL, the Gaps model) — owned by Customer Service; only the employee-to-service link is referenced
Service recovery and complaint handling — owned by Service Recovery; empowerment is noted as its precondition only
Department-level staffing specifics for housekeeping and the front office — owned by those operations topics
Individualized employment-law, wage-and-hour, payroll, or tipping-rule advice

claims.claim: The human-resources function in food service and hospitality comprises recruitment (attracting suitable applicants), selection (hiring the best-suited person), orientation, and training and development, and good HR practice is associated with higher employee satisfaction, lower staff turnover, superior customer service, and increased profitability.
In June 2025 the seasonally adjusted quits rate in leisure and hospitality was 5.0 percent, versus 2.1 percent for total nonfarm employment — more than double.

Across 2024 and 2025 the monthly total separations rate for leisure and hospitality generally ran between roughly 4.8 and 6.6 percent, compared with about 3.2 to 3.4 percent for total nonfarm employment, so the sector's turnover consistently runs well above the all-industry average.
The leisure and hospitality supersector combines Arts, Entertainment, and Recreation with Accommodation and Food Services, and is a large employer of entry-level, variable-hour, and seasonal workers.
In May 2024 the median annual wage was $68,130 for lodging managers and $65,310 for food service managers, roles that coordinate staffing and HR across a property's departments.

The service-profit chain, set out by James Heskett, Thomas Jones, Gary Loveman, W. Earl Sasser, and Leonard Schlesinger in 'Putting the Service-Profit Chain to Work' (Harvard Business Review, March-April 1994), links internal service quality to employee satisfaction, employee retention and productivity, external service value, customer satisfaction, customer loyalty, and finally revenue growth and profitability.

Empowerment — giving frontline staff authority to make decisions for the guest without escalation — speeds guest resolution and is a precondition for fast service recovery; it complements, but does not substitute for, fair pay and workable scheduling.

Hospitality is largely an experience delivered by people in real time, so the employee is a central part of the product the guest buys, making recruitment, training, and retention core management work rather than overhead.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How to state the sector's turnover magnitude precisely
positions: Monthly JOLTS quits/separations rates (directly retrieved, seasonally adjusted) show leisure and hospitality running roughly double the all-industry average
Secondary summaries cite an annualized 'total separations rate' figure (e.g., around 65-79 percent for accommodation and food services) from the BLS annual JOLTS release
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses only the monthly seasonally adjusted rates that were retrieved directly from BLS series, each dated to its release month, and frames the annual implication as an illustration in the worked example rather than asserting a specific annual figure that could not be read from a primary table (BLS blocked automated fetches of the annual tables).

unsupportedExistingClaims: The machine-generated draft was treated as editorial intent only; its boilerplate wording was discarded and not used as evidence.
correctionsNeeded: Ensured every turnover and wage figure carries a year and a named source, per subject cautions.
Kept service-quality measurement (SERVQUAL/Gaps), service recovery, and department staffing out of scope, referencing only the employee-to-service link and empowerment-as-precondition.
Gave no employment-law, payroll, or tipping advice; noted that wage/tip/overtime rules vary by jurisdiction.
rightsIssues: The 1994 HBR service-profit-chain article is copyrighted (reference-only): its framework is attributed and described, with no wording reproduced.
BLS JOLTS and OOH data are U.S. government works in the public domain; the go2HR and BCcampus texts are CC BY 4.0 (attribution recorded); no source prose was copied.
